paragraphs: Here's what Habakkuk teaches me, friend. He spent two chapters bringing hard questions to the LORD, and he ends the book with a prayer that is mostly worship. He remembers who God is and what God has done, and he asks Him, "In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (Habakkuk 3:2). When the questions are big, going back to who God is is a good place to land.

Now look at what Habakkuk does with the scary part. He hears about God going forth to save His people, and he says, "I heard and trembled within" (Habakkuk 3:16). He doesn't pretend to be calm. He says he must wait patiently for the day to come, and he waits trembling. I know a thing or two about waiting in the dark with shaky knees, and God doesn't ask you to fake it.

Then comes the part I want you to carry out of my bakery. "Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines," he says, "yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (Habakkuk 3:17-18). His joy doesn't depend on a full cookie box. It rests on the LORD, who is his strength and "makes me walk upon the heights" (Habakkuk 3:19). So when your fields look empty, baker, say the yet out loud, and maybe sing it. That's the whole reason this prayer was written for stringed instruments.
